fields.sections.0.h: Starting point of the argument: AI code should be open source
fields.sections.1.h: License laundering: unjust conversion of open-source assets
fields.sections.2.h: Legal grounds: copyright impossibility of AI-generated works
fields.sections.4.h: Gray area: code with minimal human intervention
fields.sections.0.ko: The author presents the position that all code generated by AI should be disclosed as open source. This is not merely an opinion but an argument grounded in the fairness of the technology ecosystem and legal principles. The following paragraphs develop its reasoning along two axes.
fields.sections.1.ko: AI training models have been trained on vast amounts of open-source code created by developers since the GNU Project. The problem is that this code was collected without authorization from the internet and used without source attribution. In particular, communities like Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange are published under Creative Commons licenses, which legally require attribution. Converting the collective knowledge of communities into closed proprietary code is, in fact, an act of circumventing licenses.
fields.sections.2.ko: Under US law, copyright is granted only to works created by humans. The famous 'monkey selfie' case established precedent that non-human entities cannot hold copyright, and the US Copyright Office applied this to AI. The logic is that code generated purely by AI alone, without human creative acts, cannot be subject to copyright protection. According to this principle, Wikimedia Commons also requires AI-generated images to be tagged as public domain.
fields.sections.3.ko: However, copyright law differs from country to country. Several countries, including the UK, grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. Considering these regional legal differences, the necessity for AI code disclosure becomes even stronger. The author argues that developers and companies should disclose AI-generated code under open-source licenses or CC0 (Creative Commons Zero) licenses in order to establish fair standards across all jurisdictions and fulfill responsibility to the open ecosystem that enabled AI advancement.
fields.sections.4.ko: In real development environments, code does not fall into a dichotomy of pure manual or pure automation. However, an increasing number of developers are using AI-generated outputs without properly reviewing them or modifying them to fit their needs. The author emphasizes that code where humans exert no substantial effort beyond inputting a prompt should clearly be disclosed as open source.
fields.caveat: The author's argument has gained broad sympathy in the technology community (300+ on Hacker News), but the legal status of AI copyright remains an ongoing debate across nations worldwide, and the interpretation presented here does not reflect legal consensus.
